questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. Any $4\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

II. The singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -2 & -3\end{aligned}]$ are non-negative.

III. Any $3\times 4$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Since $A$ is a $4\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 4$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 4}\times {A}_{4\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is true. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative.

- Statement III is false. Since $A$ is a $3\times 4$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $4\times 3$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $4\times 4$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{4\times 3}\times {A}_{3\times 4}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{4\times 4}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(2-\lambda ) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =8,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{8} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 8-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(8-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda -5\lambda +40-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. Any $1\times4$ matrix $A$ has at most $1$ singular value.

II. Any $4\times2$ matrix $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

III. The matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225446/assets/b8601b1e66ef1d302e7194f262f6a513063bba2114fb063c2fc16542d4684392.svg) has one negative singular value.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $1 \times 4$ matrix and $A^T$ is a $4\times 1$ matrix, $A^T \! A$ must be a $4 \times 4$ matrix: 

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times {\large 1}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 1} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A} =  
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is true. Since $A$ is a $4 \times 2$ matrix and $A^T$ is a $2\times 4$ matrix, $A^T \! A$ must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix: 

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 4}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ cannot have a negative singular value.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}0 & 1-\lambda  \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )^{2}-(1-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )^{2}-1) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda ) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -1)(\lambda -2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =2,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{2} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}

tutorials.problem:
Recall that the singular values of a real matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

Also, since $A^T \! A$ is a positive semi-definite matrix, the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A$ must be always non-negative real numbers.

Let's compute the singular values of the matrix $A,$ given by 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225446/assets/a9edbe1fee59758c9557d95ea8f62468f9f3cb98449c437a274bdbf5c30f7dc6.svg)

Now, since

- $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix, and

- $A^T$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix,

then $A^T \! A$  must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix:

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 3}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Let's now compute our singular values. First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- When listing the singular values of a matrix, we usually write them in descending order.

- If $A$ is a $m\times n$ matrix, then $A^T A$ is a $n\times n$ positive semi-definite matrix. This means that $A$ has *at most* $n$ distinct singular values.
